newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Legal tangles deter closure of Bulgarian lossmaker.
newsitem.headline: Legal tangles deter closure of Bulgarian lossmaker.

text.p: Bulgaria's closure of lossmaking state enterprises pledged to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in line with an ambitious funding programme have been detered mostly by legal tangles, an official said on Friday.

"Enterprises, which have operated for many years, with various levels of success, cannot be closed overnight," Pencho Hristov, head of the restructuring department at the Industry Ministry, told Reuters.

Of the 38 enterprises earmarked by the industry ministry, 17 have been restructureed so far. Only 12 have been closed and a further five, among which is the Plama refinery and Pirin Plast plastics producer, have been sold off to local investors.
The IMF is expected to evaluate Bulgaria's fulfilment of reform targets and decide shortly on a $115 million second tranche of funding which is crucial for the country's crumbling economy.
Under a reform agreement sealed with the IMF in July, Sofia stands to receive $580 billion over 20 months on completion of specific reform stages.
The second $115 million tranche was delayed by the Fund until the government closed or privatised 64 lossmakers by end-September.

"We try to choose the best solution for each enterprise as some of these current lossmakers have a very valuable and sophisticated equipment and could make profits if their debts were written off or paid by an interested investor," said Hristov.

The ministry seeks alternative solutions to closures in a bid to save productions considered viable which have suffered losses because of the country's tedious and sporadic transition to market economy, he added.
Offers to investors and mergers with a larger profit-making company are the alternatives, said Hristov.
"Our aim is to let viable firms which suffer temporary problems continue operating under a more healthy management," he added.

Several of seven military equipment plants listed for closure will be merged with bigger plants and the ministry will freeze the remaining few of the seven military plants. Hristov declined to elaborate.
For a further 18 state firms privatisation procedures were opened.
Of 11,000 employed in the 38 lossmakers, some 4,200 employees have been shed so far, said Hristov.
The ministry plans to close down additional 40 industrial lossmakers until the year-end, said Hristov.
It is yet unclear whether the IMF will accept Bulgaria's justifications for delayed completion of reform targets.

Sofia, grappling with bank insolvency and the collapse of the lev, which plunged from 70 to the dollar in January to about 230 this week, has effectively closed nine banks by putting them under state supervision and raised the central bank interest rate to a record high of 300 percent.

With current high rates banks have little hope of receiving interest on loans given to those lossmakers, but in cases where the firms are bought the banks agree with the new buyers for repayment of the priniciple and reschedule the interest.
"Bulgaria's is paying a high price for six years of delayed privatisation. Now the state will receive a much lower value for its assets," said Hristov.
